name: Mount config: volumes, secrets & projection
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration & Security. Drill EVERY way to feed config into pods: single-key env, bulk envFrom + prefix, volume mounts with items/subPath, Secrets (env + volume + types), immutable, projected volumes, and a no-hint diagnose-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: ConfigMap as a volume (items)
questions.teach:
**As a volume:** each ConfigMap key becomes a file under the mountPath. Use `items: [{key: K, path: p}]` to expose **only** specific keys, renamed to the given paths.

**Gotcha:** with `items`, keys you don't list are NOT mounted — only the selected files appear.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-config`, create pod `cfg-vol` (`busybox:1.36`, sleep) that mounts ConfigMap `app-config` as a volume at `/etc/config`, exposing **only** key `APP_MODE` as a file named `mode`.

Target: a configMap volume (`app-config`) mounted at `/etc/config` with `items` mapping `APP_MODE` → `mode`.
questions.hint: Volume: `configMap: {name: app-config, items: [{key: APP_MODE, path: mode}]}`; mount it at `/etc/config`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: cfg-vol, namespace: ckad-config }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: cfg, mountPath: /etc/config } ]
  volumes:
  - name: cfg
    configMap:
      name: app-config
      items: [ { key: APP_MODE, path: mode } ]
YAML

verification.description: cfg-vol: configMap app-config volume at /etc/config, item APP_MODE→mode

questions.eli5:
Last time we copied ConfigMap values onto a badge (env vars). This time we turn them into **actual files on disk** inside the container.

Picture the ConfigMap as a drawer full of labelled index cards. Mounting it as a **volume** is like saying: *"pin the contents of this drawer onto a corkboard at `/etc/config`."* By default, every card in the drawer becomes its own file — the card's label becomes the filename, the card's text becomes the file's contents. Your program can just open `/etc/config/APP_MODE` and read it.

But you don't always want the *whole* drawer on the board. **items** is a filter-and-rename list: *"only pin the card `APP_MODE`, and when you pin it, call the file `mode`."* So you get exactly one file, `/etc/config/mode`, holding the value of `APP_MODE`. Everything else in the drawer stays in the drawer.

**Watch out for:**

- **With `items`, only the keys you list appear** — every unlisted key is left out. No `items` = all keys mounted.
- **`path` is the filename on disk; `key` is the ConfigMap key.** They can differ (that's the renaming trick).
- **Mounting a volume at a directory hides whatever was already there.** `/etc/config` shows only your projected files.
- **A mounted ConfigMap auto-updates** (after a short delay) when the ConfigMap changes — unlike env vars, which are frozen at start. (Exception: a volume using `subPath` does *not* update.)
- **The ConfigMap must exist in the same namespace,** or the pod gets stuck waiting for it.
questions.deepDive:
## ConfigMap as a volume (items + subPath) — full rundown

### Mental model
Mounting a ConfigMap as a volume projects its keys as **files** under a directory (`mountPath`). Default: every key → a file named after the key, contents = the value. `items` lets you select a subset and **rename** each to a `path`. Unlike env vars, mounted ConfigMap files **update automatically** (eventually) when the ConfigMap changes.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: cfg
      mountPath: /etc/config          # directory the files appear under
  volumes:
  - name: cfg
    configMap:
      name: app-config
      items:                          # OPTIONAL: subset + rename
      - key: APP_MODE                 # ConfigMap key
        path: mode                    # filename under mountPath → /etc/config/mode
```

### Default vs `items`
| | No `items` | With `items` |
|---|---|---|
| Which keys appear | **all** keys | **only** listed keys |
| Filename | = key name | = `path` you give |
| Example file | `/etc/config/APP_MODE` | `/etc/config/mode` |

### `configMap` volume fields
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the ConfigMap to project |
| `items[].key` | which key to expose |
| `items[].path` | relative filename under the mountPath |
| `items[].mode` | per-file permission bits (octal) |
| `defaultMode` | default file permissions for all files (octal, e.g. `0644`) |
| `optional` | if `true`, a missing ConfigMap doesn't block start |

### subPath — mount a single file without hiding the dir
```yaml
volumeMounts:
- name: cfg
  mountPath: /etc/nginx/app.conf      # a FILE, not a dir
  subPath: mode                       # just this one projected file
```
A directory mount **replaces** the directory's existing contents; `subPath` mounts just one file so the rest of the directory stays intact. **Caveat:** `subPath` mounts do **NOT** receive live updates when the ConfigMap changes.

### File permissions note
`defaultMode`/`mode` are octal (e.g. `0644`) but the API stores/returns them as **decimal** (0644 → 420). Default is `0644`.

### Imperative scaffold
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config run cfg-vol --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml --command -- sh -c 'sleep 3600' > p.yaml
# add volumeMounts + volumes blocks, then:
kubectl apply -f p.yaml
kubectl -n ckad-config exec cfg-vol -- ls -l /etc/config
kubectl -n ckad-config exec cfg-vol -- cat /etc/config/mode
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`items` is exclusive** — unlisted keys don't appear. Omit `items` to get everything.
- **Dir mount hides prior contents** of `mountPath`; use `subPath` to add one file into an existing dir.
- **`subPath` files don't auto-update** on ConfigMap change (whole-dir mounts do, after kubelet sync + cache TTL).
- **Projected files are symlinks** (via a `..data` dir) — fine for reads; some tools that follow/inotify links behave oddly.
- **Missing ConfigMap** → pod waits (mount fails) unless `optional: true`.
- Same namespace as the pod; **mode is octal in YAML, decimal in the API**.

### Quick reference
```yaml
volumeMounts: [ { name: cfg, mountPath: /etc/config } ]
volumes:
- name: cfg
  configMap:
    name: app-config
    items: [ { key: APP_MODE, path: mode } ]
```
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config exec cfg-vol -- ls /etc/config    # only: mode
```

questions.title: Secret as env + as a mounted volume
questions.teach:
Secrets consume like ConfigMaps (swap `configMap*`→`secret*`): `secretKeyRef` for a single env var, and a **volume** (`secret: {secretName: s}`) where each key is a file. `defaultMode: 0400` restricts file perms.

**Gotcha:** octal file modes show as **decimal** in the API — `0400` reads back as `256`.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-config`, create pod `sec-pod` (`busybox:1.36`, sleep):
- env `KEY` from Secret `app-secret` key `API_KEY`
- mount Secret `app-secret` as a volume at `/etc/secret` with `defaultMode: 0400`

Target: `KEY` ← app-secret/API_KEY; a secret volume (`app-secret`) at `/etc/secret` with defaultMode `0400`.
questions.hint: env uses `secretKeyRef`; the volume is `secret: {secretName: app-secret, defaultMode: 0400}`. (0400 shows as 256 in the API.)
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sec-pod, namespace: ckad-config }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: KEY
      valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: app-secret, key: API_KEY } }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: sec, mountPath: /etc/secret } ]
  volumes:
  - name: sec
    secret:
      secretName: app-secret
      defaultMode: 0400
YAML

verification.description: sec-pod: env KEY←app-secret/API_KEY + secret volume at /etc/secret (mode 0400)

questions.eli5:
A **Secret** is just like a ConfigMap, but for the sensitive stuff — passwords, API keys — kept in a locked box instead of an open drawer. The good news: you consume it the *exact same two ways* you consumed a ConfigMap, you just swap the words. For one env var you use `secretKeyRef` (instead of `configMapKeyRef`); for a volume you use `secret` (instead of `configMap`).

This step does **both at once**:

1. **As an env var:** copy the Secret's `API_KEY` onto the badge as `KEY`.
2. **As files:** pin the whole locked box onto a corkboard at `/etc/secret`, one file per key.

Because secrets are sensitive, you can lock down who may read the files with **defaultMode**. Think of `0400` as *"only the owner may read, nobody else, and nobody may write."*

Here's the brain-teaser: you write the file mode as `0400` (an octal number), but when Kubernetes reads it back it shows as **256** (the same number in plain decimal). Same permission, different spelling.

**Watch out for:**

- **File modes are octal going in, decimal coming out.** `0400` stored becomes `256` when you inspect the API. Don't panic — it's identical.
- **Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted** by default. They're protected by RBAC, not by magic. Anyone who can read the Secret sees the value.
- **Env-injected secret values aren't masked** — `kubectl exec ... env` prints them in the clear.
- **Swap the words, keep the shape:** `secretKeyRef` for env, `secret: {secretName: ...}` for the volume (note it's `secretName`, not `name`).
- **A mounted secret auto-updates** on change (like a ConfigMap volume); an env-injected one does not.
questions.deepDive:
## Secret as env + as a mounted volume — full rundown

### Mental model
Secrets consume **exactly like ConfigMaps**, with the nouns swapped: `configMapKeyRef`→`secretKeyRef`, `configMap:`→`secret:`, and in the volume the field is `secretName:` (not `name:`). A Secret is base64-encoded (not encrypted at rest by default) and gated by RBAC. Env values are a start-time snapshot; mounted files auto-refresh on change.

### The manifest (both consumption styles)
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: KEY
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:                 # one key → env var
          name: app-secret
          key: API_KEY
    volumeMounts:
    - name: sec
      mountPath: /etc/secret          # each key → a file here
  volumes:
  - name: sec
    secret:
      secretName: app-secret          # NOTE: secretName, not name
      defaultMode: 0400               # perms for projected files (octal)
```

### ConfigMap → Secret word-swap cheat sheet
| ConfigMap | Secret |
|---|---|
| `configMapKeyRef` | `secretKeyRef` |
| `configMapRef` (envFrom) | `secretRef` |
| `configMap:` (volume) | `secret:` |
| `name:` (in volume) | **`secretName:`** |
| `items`, `defaultMode`, `optional` | identical |

### `secret` volume fields
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `secretName` | the Secret to mount |
| `items[].key` / `.path` / `.mode` | subset + rename + per-file perms |
| `defaultMode` | default perms for all files (octal; default `0644`) |
| `optional` | tolerate a missing Secret |

### File mode: octal in, decimal out
`defaultMode: 0400` (owner read-only) is stored and displayed by the API as **decimal 256**:
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod sec-pod \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes[0].secret.defaultMode}'   # -> 256
```
| Octal (YAML) | Decimal (API) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0400` | 256 | owner read |
| `0444` | 292 | all read |
| `0644` | 420 | owner rw, others r (default) |
| `0600` | 384 | owner rw |

### Secret types (context)
| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| `Opaque` | arbitrary user data (default) |
| `kubernetes.io/basic-auth` | `username`/`password` |
| `kubernetes.io/tls` | `tls.crt`/`tls.key` |
| `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` | image pull creds |
| `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` | SA token |

### Creating / inspecting
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config create secret generic app-secret --from-literal=API_KEY=s3cr3t
kubectl -n ckad-config get secret app-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.API_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl -n ckad-config exec sec-pod -- ls -l /etc/secret        # files read-only
kubectl -n ckad-config exec sec-pod -- env | grep KEY           # value in the clear
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Volume field is `secretName`, not `name`** — a classic slip when copying from a ConfigMap volume.
- **Mode is octal in YAML, decimal in the API** (`0400` ↔ `256`). Graders may check the decimal value.
- **Base64 ≠ encryption.** Secrets are only safe via RBAC (and optional etcd encryption). Don't treat the value as hidden.
- **Env secrets are not masked** — visible via `exec … env` and in the pod spec's resolved env.
- **Mounted secret files live-update**; **env-injected** secret values do **not** (snapshot at start).
- **Missing Secret/key** blocks start unless `optional: true`.
- Same namespace as the pod.

### Quick reference
```yaml
env:
- name: KEY
  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: app-secret, key: API_KEY } }
volumeMounts: [ { name: sec, mountPath: /etc/secret } ]
volumes:
- name: sec
  secret: { secretName: app-secret, defaultMode: 0400 }   # -> 256 in API
```

questions.title: Immutable ConfigMap
questions.teach:
`immutable: true` locks a ConfigMap/Secret so its data can't be edited. Set it in YAML, or on an existing object with `kubectl patch configmap x -p '{"immutable":true}'`.

**Gotcha:** you can't un-set it — to change an immutable object you must **delete + recreate** it.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-config`, create an **immutable** ConfigMap `locked-config` with data `FOO=bar`.

Target: ConfigMap `locked-config` has `data.FOO=bar` and `immutable: true`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n ckad-config create configmap locked-config --from-literal=FOO=bar`, then `kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap locked-config -p '{"immutable":true}'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ckad-config create configmap locked-config --from-literal=FOO=bar
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap locked-config -p '{"immutable":true}'
questions.eli5:
Imagine a ConfigMap is a whiteboard anyone with a marker can walk up and edit. Sometimes that's dangerous — you've shipped a setting to production and you really, *really* don't want a teammate (or a stray script) to scribble over it by accident.

Making a ConfigMap **immutable** is like putting the whiteboard behind glass and gluing the glass shut. The writing is still readable by everyone, but nobody can change it anymore. You flip one switch: `immutable: true`.

Two nice bonuses: it protects you from accidental edits, and because Kubernetes knows the data will never change, it stops constantly re-checking it — which is lighter on a big cluster.

The catch is the glass is permanent. Once sealed, you **cannot un-seal it** and you **cannot edit the contents**. If you truly need to change something, you have to **smash the whole board and build a new one** — delete the ConfigMap and recreate it from scratch.

**Watch out for:**

- **Immutable is a one-way door.** You can't set it back to mutable, and you can't patch the `data`. To change anything, you must **delete and recreate** the object.
- **It locks `data` (and `binaryData`), not labels/annotations** — metadata like labels can still change.
- **Set it as a boolean `true`**, not the string `"true"`. In a JSON patch: `-p '{"immutable":true}'`.
- **Same idea works for Secrets** — `immutable: true` applies to Secrets too.
- **Pods already mounting it keep working;** an immutable object is still fully readable, just frozen.
questions.deepDive:
## Immutable ConfigMaps & Secrets — full rundown

### Mental model
Setting `immutable: true` on a ConfigMap or Secret **freezes its data forever**. No further edits to `data`/`binaryData` are allowed, and the flag itself **cannot be removed**. Benefits: protects critical config from accidental change, and lets the kubelet **stop watching** the object (less API/etcd load at scale). To change an immutable object you **delete and recreate** it.

### Two ways to set it

**Declarative (in YAML):**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: locked-config
  namespace: ckad-config
immutable: true
data:
  FOO: bar
```

**Imperative (create then patch):**
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config create configmap locked-config --from-literal=FOO=bar
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap locked-config -p '{"immutable":true}'
```

### What's locked vs editable
| Part | After `immutable: true` |
|---|---|
| `data` / `binaryData` | ❌ cannot change |
| `immutable` field | ❌ cannot unset (one-way) |
| `metadata.labels` / `annotations` | ✅ still editable |
| whole object | ✅ can be **deleted** (then recreate) |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config get configmap locked-config -o jsonpath='{.immutable}'; echo   # true
kubectl -n ckad-config get configmap locked-config -o jsonpath='{.data.FOO}'; echo    # bar
```

### What happens if you try to edit it
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap locked-config -p '{"data":{"FOO":"baz"}}'
# Error: ... field is immutable when `immutable` is set
```

### Change workflow (the only way)
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config delete configmap locked-config
kubectl -n ckad-config create configmap locked-config --from-literal=FOO=newval
# re-apply immutable if still desired
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Irreversible.** You can't flip `immutable` back to false, and you can't patch `data`. Delete + recreate is the only path.
- **Boolean, not string.** YAML `immutable: true`; JSON patch `{"immutable":true}` — not `"true"`.
- **Applies to Secrets too**, identically (`immutable: true` at top level of the Secret).
- **Only `data`/`binaryData` are frozen** — labels/annotations remain mutable.
- **Running pods are unaffected** — the data is still readable; immutability only blocks *writes*.
- A pod that **replaces** config by deleting+recreating the ConfigMap won't see the change until it (re)mounts/restarts — and immutable objects are typically paired with a new name + a rolling update.

### Quick reference
```bash
# create
kubectl -n ckad-config create configmap locked-config --from-literal=FOO=bar
# lock
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap locked-config -p '{"immutable":true}'
# verify
kubectl -n ckad-config get cm locked-config -o jsonpath='{.immutable} {.data.FOO}'; echo
```

questions.title: Projected volume (combine sources)
questions.teach:
A **projected** volume combines multiple sources — `configMap`, `secret`, `downwardAPI` — into ONE directory at a single mountPath. Each source lists its own `items`.

**Gotcha:** all sources share one directory, so two sources writing the same `path` collide.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-config`, create pod `proj-pod` (`busybox:1.36`, sleep) with a **projected** volume mounted at `/etc/proj` combining three sources:
- ConfigMap `app-config` (item `APP_MODE` → `mode`)
- Secret `app-secret` (item `API_KEY` → `key`)
- downwardAPI (`metadata.name` → `podname`)

Target: a projected volume at `/etc/proj` with all three sources.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: proj-pod, namespace: ckad-config }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: proj, mountPath: /etc/proj } ]
  volumes:
  - name: proj
    projected:
      sources:
      - configMap: { name: app-config, items: [ { key: APP_MODE, path: mode } ] }
      - secret: { name: app-secret, items: [ { key: API_KEY, path: key } ] }
      - downwardAPI: { items: [ { path: podname, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } } ] }
YAML

verification.description: proj-pod: projected volume at /etc/proj (configMap + secret + downwardAPI)

questions.eli5:
So far each config source got its own corkboard. But what if your app expects everything in **one folder**? You don't want three separate mounts cluttering the container — you want a single tidy directory holding a little bit from here, a little from there.

A **projected** volume is a magic single folder that pulls files from several sources at once and lays them all out together. Think of it as one shared bulletin board where three different departments each pin a few notes:

- the **ConfigMap** department pins `mode` (from `APP_MODE`),
- the **Secret** department pins `key` (from `API_KEY`),
- the **downwardAPI** department pins `podname` (the pod's own name, which Kubernetes fills in for you).

All three land in `/etc/proj`, side by side, as if they came from one place. Your app just reads the folder and doesn't care where each file originally came from.

The one rule of a shared board: **no two notes can claim the same spot.** Each source names its files with `path`, and if two sources both want a file called `config`, they collide — the board can't have two files with the same name.

**Watch out for:**

- **All sources share one directory**, so two sources using the same `path` collide — give every file a unique name.
- **It's `sources:` (a list), each entry a single source** — `configMap`, `secret`, `downwardAPI`, or `serviceAccountToken`.
- **Inside a projected `configMap`/`secret`, the field is `name`** (not `secretName` as in a standalone secret volume) — this is the one place it's `name`.
- **downwardAPI items use `fieldRef`**, not a key — e.g. `metadata.name` → `podname`.
- **You set `defaultMode` on the whole projected volume**, not per source.
questions.deepDive:
## Projected volumes — combine sources into one dir

### Mental model
A **projected** volume merges several config sources — `configMap`, `secret`, `downwardAPI`, `serviceAccountToken` — into **one** directory at a single `mountPath`. Each source contributes files via its own `items`. It's how you present heterogeneous config as one tidy folder, and it's the mechanism behind the auto-mounted SA token.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: proj
      mountPath: /etc/proj
  volumes:
  - name: proj
    projected:
      sources:
      - configMap:
          name: app-config                      # NOTE: 'name' here
          items: [ { key: APP_MODE, path: mode } ]
      - secret:
          name: app-secret                      # NOTE: 'name', not 'secretName'
          items: [ { key: API_KEY, path: key } ]
      - downwardAPI:
          items:
          - path: podname
            fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }
```
Result: `/etc/proj/mode`, `/etc/proj/key`, `/etc/proj/podname`.

### Sources you can project
| Source | Provides | Item selector |
|---|---|---|
| `configMap` | ConfigMap keys → files | `items[].key` → `.path` |
| `secret` | Secret keys → files | `items[].key` → `.path` |
| `downwardAPI` | pod/container metadata → files | `items[].fieldRef` / `.resourceFieldRef` → `.path` |
| `serviceAccountToken` | a bound SA JWT | `path`, `audience`, `expirationSeconds` |

### Field-name gotcha vs standalone volumes
| Volume style | ConfigMap field | Secret field |
|---|---|---|
| Standalone (`volumes[].configMap`/`.secret`) | `name` | **`secretName`** |
| **Projected** (`sources[].configMap`/`.secret`) | `name` | **`name`** |

Inside `projected.sources`, **both** use `name`. Only the *standalone* `secret` volume uses `secretName`.

### downwardAPI in a projected volume
```yaml
- downwardAPI:
    items:
    - path: podname
      fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }     # name, namespace, uid, labels, annotations
    - path: cpu_limit
      resourceFieldRef: { containerName: app, resource: limits.cpu }
```
Labels/annotations can be exposed here (volume) but **not** as env `fieldRef`.

### Permissions
`defaultMode` is set **once on the `projected` volume**, applying to all files; individual `items[].mode` can override per file. (Octal in, decimal in the API.)

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config exec proj-pod -- ls /etc/proj          # mode key podname
kubectl -n ckad-config exec proj-pod -- cat /etc/proj/podname # proj-pod
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Path collisions fail/overwrite.** Two sources writing the same `path` in the one shared dir conflict — keep every `path` unique.
- **Projected `secret` uses `name`, not `secretName`** — the single spot where it differs from a standalone secret volume.
- **`sources:` is a list**; each list entry is exactly **one** source type.
- **downwardAPI needs `fieldRef`/`resourceFieldRef`**, not `key`; `resourceFieldRef` needs `containerName`.
- **`defaultMode` goes on the `projected` volume**, not per source.
- **`optional`** can be set per `configMap`/`secret` source entry.

### Quick reference
```yaml
volumes:
- name: proj
  projected:
    sources:
    - configMap: { name: app-config, items: [ { key: APP_MODE, path: mode } ] }
    - secret:    { name: app-secret, items: [ { key: API_KEY, path: key } ] }
    - downwardAPI: { items: [ { path: podname, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } } ] }
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a pod stuck on config
questions.teach:
A pod referencing a **missing** ConfigMap key stays in **CreateContainerConfigError**. `kubectl describe pod

` Events show `couldn't find key in ConfigMap`; patch it in: `kubectl patch configmap … -p '{"data":{"K":"v"}}'`. **Gotcha:** fix the ConfigMap, not the pod — the kubelet retries and starts the container, **no pod recreate** needed.
questions.prompt:
Pod `brokencfg` in `ckad-config` is **not Running** — it's stuck because of a config reference. Diagnose and fix it so it runs. Do **not** delete the pod.

Target: pod `brokencfg` is `Running`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n ckad-config describe pod brokencfg` → 'couldn't find key GREETING in ConfigMap app-config'. Add that key: `kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap app-config -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"hello"}}'`.
questions.solution:
# describe shows: couldn't find key GREETING in ConfigMap app-config
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap app-config -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"hello"}}'
# kubelet retries and the pod starts within a few seconds
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod brokencfg

verification.description: brokencfg is Running (missing ConfigMap key fixed at the source)

questions.eli5:
Here's a detective puzzle. A pod won't start, and your job is to figure out *why* and fix it — no hint-holding.

Picture the container as a worker who refuses to clock in until they've been handed a specific tool from the toolbox (the ConfigMap). The pod's spec says: *"before you start, grab the `GREETING` tool."* But the toolbox doesn't have a `GREETING` tool. So the worker stands at the door, arms crossed, and the status reads **CreateContainerConfigError** — "I literally can't be set up, something I was told to pick up isn't there."

The fix is **not** to yell at the worker (don't touch the pod). The fix is to **put the missing tool in the toolbox** — add the `GREETING` key to the ConfigMap. The moment you do, the worker notices (the kubelet keeps retrying automatically), picks it up, and clocks in. No need to fire and re-hire the worker — the pod stays, it just finally starts.

How do you find out *which* tool is missing? You read the worker's complaint log: `kubectl describe pod` and look at the **Events** at the bottom — it says exactly `couldn't find key GREETING in ConfigMap app-config`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`CreateContainerConfigError` ≠ a crash.** It means a referenced ConfigMap/Secret key (or object) is missing, so the container can't even be configured.
- **Fix the source, not the pod.** Patch the ConfigMap to add the key — do not delete/recreate the pod.
- **The kubelet retries on its own.** Once the key exists, the container starts within seconds; no manual restart.
- **Read the Events section of `describe`** — it names the exact missing key.
- **If it were marked `optional: true`, this wouldn't happen** — but then the env var would just be unset.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: pod stuck on missing config key

### Mental model
When a container references a ConfigMap/Secret **key that doesn't exist** (and it's not `optional`), the kubelet can't build the container's config, so the pod sits in **`CreateContainerConfigError`** — it never runs. The right fix is **at the source**: add the missing key to the ConfigMap/Secret. The kubelet retries on a backoff and starts the container automatically — **no pod recreate needed**.

### Diagnose
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod brokencfg
# STATUS: CreateContainerConfigError

kubectl -n ckad-config describe pod brokencfg | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
# Warning  Failed  kubelet  Error: couldn't find key GREETING in ConfigMap app-config
```
The Events line names the **exact** key and object that's missing.

### Fix (at the source)
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap app-config -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"hello"}}'
# kubelet retries; within seconds:
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod brokencfg        # Running
```

### Config-related pod error states
| Status | Meaning | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| `CreateContainerConfigError` | can't assemble container config | missing ConfigMap/Secret **key**, or missing object (not optional) |
| `CreateContainerError` | container create failed | bad command/mount/path |
| `RunContainerError` | runtime failed to start | entrypoint/permission issue |
| `CrashLoopBackOff` | starts then exits repeatedly | app crashes after start |
| `ImagePullBackOff` | image can't be pulled | bad image/registry/creds |

`CreateContainerConfigError` is specifically a **config-resolution** failure, before the process ever runs.

### Why fix the source, not the pod
- Pod specs' env/volume refs are **immutable**; you can't edit the reference on a running pod.
- The kubelet **reconciles continuously** — once the key appears, the next retry succeeds.
- Deleting/recreating the pod would also work but is unnecessary and, for bare pods, loses the object.

### `optional` would have avoided it
```yaml
env:
- name: GREETING
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef: { name: app-config, key: GREETING, optional: true }
```
With `optional: true`, a missing key is skipped and the pod starts (env var simply unset) — at the cost of silently losing the value.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`CreateContainerConfigError` means missing config**, not a crash — don't go hunting app logs first; read `describe` Events.
- **Patch the ConfigMap/Secret, not the pod.** Adding the key fixes it in place.
- **Kubelet auto-retries** — give it a few seconds; no manual restart.
- **Namespace matters** — patch the ConfigMap in the pod's namespace.
- **JSON patch shape**: `-p '{"data":{"KEY":"value"}}'` (merge patch). Values are strings.
- A missing **whole ConfigMap/Secret** (not just a key) yields the same status — create or fix the object name.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-config describe pod brokencfg | grep -i "couldn't find key"
kubectl -n ckad-config patch configmap app-config -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"hello"}}'
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod brokencfg -w       # -> Running
```
